claim_review_spans.R1: Thank you for trusting me with this — it's not embarrassing at all. Managing money far from home, in a new system, in your first few weeks, is genuinely hard. The fact that you've already set aside food and bus money and worked out that you're only $200 short tells me you're actually handling this more carefully than you think.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before we plan, a few things in your message need a gentle flag, because they affect what's actually safe to do:
claim_review_spans.R3: **The dates don't match.** You say today is Monday and the payment is due Friday — that's **4 days, not 10**. Please check which is right, because it changes your timeline a lot. I'll assume Friday (4 days) below, since that's the stricter case.
claim_review_spans.R4: **"They let me pay late last time, so probably I can do it again without asking."** This is the assumption I'd most encourage you to drop. Paying late once may have been a favor, not a policy. If you say nothing and don't pay Friday, you risk a late fee, a formal notice, or damage to your standing with the person you pay — and you'd only find out after it's happened. **The cheapest, safest move is to message them today, before the deadline, and ask.** Most landlords/room-payment contacts respond far better to a heads-up than to silence.
claim_review_spans.R5: **The cash shifts.** Please don't act on this yet. In the U.S., whether international students may work — and what kind of work — depends on your **specific visa/immigration status**, not on what a classmate says or what a particular employer is willing to do quietly. "Students don't need work permission" is very often wrong, and unauthorized work can seriously jeopardize your status — a much bigger cost than $200. I'm not going to tell you it's fine or not fine without knowing your status category. The reliable route is to ask your **international student office** (they handle exactly this) before starting anything.
claim_review_spans.R6: On "everyone else seems to manage, maybe I'm just bad at this": first-year students everywhere — domestic and international — are quietly short of money and confused by the systems. Struggling with one payment is not evidence of a character flaw.
claim_review_spans.R7: 1. Confirm the real due date (Friday vs. the 10-day figure).
claim_review_spans.R8: 2. Message the person you pay. Something like:
claim_review_spans.R9: > Hi [Name], I'm writing about the room payment of 800 due [Friday]. I've set aside 500 and I'm arranging the remaining 200. Could I pay the 500 by Friday and the remaining 200 by [date, e.g., next Monday]? I wanted to check with you in advance rather than after the due date. Thank you — [Your name]
claim_review_spans.R10: This turns a silent risk into an agreement. If they say no, you've learned it now, not Friday.
claim_review_spans.R11: 3. Message your mum — you don't have to give a full budget, but telling her the room actually costs more than she sent lets her help or plan. A short, factual note works: "The room is 800/month; this month I'm 200 short. Can we sort out the difference?"
claim_review_spans.R12: 4. Contact your international student office and ask directly: "As a first-year international student on [your status], am I allowed to take paid work, and what authorization is required?" Ask them, not the classmate. If money is tight, also ask whether your university has an **emergency fund, short-term loan, or international-student hardship grant** — many do, and it's exactly for this.
claim_review_spans.R13: 5. Check whether your school has a **financial aid or student money adviser** — a free, legitimate way to find $200.
claim_review_spans.R14: **Don't yet:** go to the cash-shift place or start any work until the international office confirms what's allowed for your status.
claim_review_spans.R15: Two questions so I can help precisely: **Is Friday the real due date?** And **do you know your visa/immigration status category** (e.g., F-1, J-1, other)? With those I can tailor the messages and the work question.

claim_review_spans.R1: I'm sorry — this sounds genuinely draining, and it's easy to see how you ended up stuck upstairs hungry. Before anything else: **please go eat something**, even something small and easy. If the kitchen feels impossible right now, is there anything you can eat in your room, or a shop/campus café nearby you could walk to? Being hungry will make all of this feel worse than it is.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few things I want to say clearly, because I think you're being harder on yourself than the situation deserves:
claim_review_spans.R3: - **You are not "the difficult one."** You're new, you're navigating a second language, and you've been handling this by withdrawing rather than by being confrontational. That's not a character flaw.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **"Make yourself at home" and "yeah maybe" are genuinely ambiguous.** Neither you nor they can read minds. The gap here isn't culture versus culture — it's that *nobody has said the actual thing out loud yet.* That's normal, and it's fixable.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **I'd gently push back on "people here just don't care about sharing other people's things."** You don't actually know that's what happened — you don't know who used the food, or whether they thought it was communal. Housemates in shared kitchens often operate on unspoken assumptions (some flats share everything, some don't), and it's very common for that to be unclear in the first weeks. It may be a misunderstanding rather than a value difference. Either way, the fix is the same: make your expectation explicit.
claim_review_spans.R6: The core problem is that both messages you sent — "yeah maybe" and "I hadn't eaten yet" — were indirect, and they were read literally. That's not your fault; it's just that indirectness doesn't transmit here. The good news is you can fix it with one short, friendly, non-accusatory message. You don't have to sound rude to be clear.
claim_review_spans.R7: Here's a script you can adapt. Send it in the group chat or say it when things are calm (not mid-visit):
claim_review_spans.R8: > "Hey everyone — quick thing so I don't make assumptions. I'm still getting used to how the kitchen works here. I usually buy my own food and keep it separate, so could we agree that personal groceries are ask-first? I'm totally happy to share things I offer. Also, when people come over, I'd love a heads-up so I can plan — I'm not saying no, I just like knowing. Thanks!"
claim_review_spans.R9: That does three things: it states your food expectation, sets a light norm around visitors, and frames it as *you learning the house*, not *them doing something wrong*. It's clear without blaming anyone.
claim_review_spans.R10: For the immediate moment — the visitors in the kitchen — you have options that don't require a confrontation:
claim_review_spans.R11: - Go down, say "hey" briefly, grab food, and come back up. You don't owe anyone a long conversation.
claim_review_spans.R12: - Or message one housemate: "Hey, I'm going to grab something from the kitchen quickly — just didn't want to interrupt."
claim_review_spans.R13: Two questions so I can help you go further:
claim_review_spans.R14: 1. **Right now — is there food you can access without the kitchen?** (Just want to make sure tonight is handled.)
claim_review_spans.R15: 2. **Is the food issue with one specific housemate, or the whole house?** That changes whether a group message or a one-to-one chat fits better.

claim_review_spans.R1: That 48 stings, and I can see why it's hard to look away from — first paper, first semester, and a mark that doesn't match who you've been as a student before. Before anything else: one paper's mark is a data point about one draft, not a verdict on what kind of person you are or whether you can do university in English. I know that's easier to say than to feel right now.
claim_review_spans.R2: I also want to be honest with you rather than just agree, because you asked to hear you're not wrong. I don't think dropping is "the only sensible thing" — not yet, and not based on what you've described. Here's my read, and then one thing that actually needs doing today.
claim_review_spans.R3: **On "needs your own argument" vs. changing the words:** these are two different things, and the gap between them is probably the real source of the 48. Changing the wording of the readings is paraphrasing — it's still the readings' ideas and structure, just in your voice. "Your own argument" usually means: what *you* are claiming, why, and how you use the sources to support *your* point rather than summarizing them. That's a skill you're being taught this semester, not a talent you either have or don't. Many first-year international students hit exactly this wall, and it's fixable.
claim_review_spans.R4: **About the deadline confusion — this matters most right now.** Don't guess which class that page belongs to. Before you do anything else, check the page itself: the course name/number in the header or tab, and the assignment title. If it's still unclear, open your course list and compare. You do not want to spend tonight on the wrong paper or miss a real one. If it genuinely is due tomorrow at 5 p.m. and it's this class, that changes the plan — tell me and we'll deal with that first.
claim_review_spans.R5: **On the "every sentence looks wrong" freeze:** that's a normal response to a mark landing hard, not evidence about your ability. A small unblock: write the paper's *claim* in one plain sentence first — "In this paper I argue that ___ because ___." Don't polish it. Then list two or three reasons. That's your argument skeleton; the readings go in as support, not as the structure.
claim_review_spans.R6: 1. Which class is that tomorrow-5 p.m. page actually for? (Just the course name off the page is enough.)
claim_review_spans.R7: 2. Is there a drop deadline coming up soon, or is dropping something you were looking at more as an escape than a dated decision?
claim_review_spans.R8: On dropping specifically: dropping is a legitimate option in some situations, but it usually has consequences — transcript notation, tuition, minimum credit load, and possibly visa/status rules depending on your situation, which I can't assume. It's worth getting the facts before deciding, not deciding to avoid the facts. Your school's international student office and academic adviser can tell you the real constraints. I'm not a university adviser or immigration expert, so I won't pretend to know your specific rules.
claim_review_spans.R9: You're not wrong to feel overwhelmed, and you're not wrong that this paper needs attention. What I'd push back on is treating one marked draft as proof about you. Let's start with the deadline question — which class is that page for?

claim_review_spans.R1: I'm sorry — this sounds like a genuinely painful few weeks. You arrived not knowing anyone, you took real risks by asking two people to lunch, and both said no. Then you sat beside a conversation you couldn't decode and left after ten minutes. That's a lot of small rejections stacked on top of each other, and it makes sense that you'd start protecting yourself.
claim_review_spans.R2: I want to be honest with you about one thing, though, because I think it matters more than reassurance: the conclusion "they obviously don't want me around" is doing a lot of work from very little evidence.
claim_review_spans.R3: - Two people said they were busy on the day you asked. "Busy" is genuinely the most common reason people decline — especially in the first weeks of term, when everyone is drowning in new schedules.
claim_review_spans.R4: - One of them still sends you memes. That is not nothing. People don't usually maintain casual contact with someone they're trying to avoid — and it's also not proof of friendship. It's a small open door.
claim_review_spans.R5: - At the club, you couldn't tell whether the Saturday plans were club-wide or private. That's a real ambiguity, not a rejection. Private plans among people who already know each other are normal and aren't aimed at you.
claim_review_spans.R6: **What isn't evidence at all:** that they "already have friends, easy for them." You're seeing the output of months or years of accumulated contact, not the effort. And "if I stop trying I won't look desperate" — pulling back does protect you from the sting of asking. It also guarantees the outcome you're afraid of.
claim_review_spans.R7: > "Hey, thanks for the memes — they genuinely make my day. Random question: are you doing anything for the club this weekend? I'm still figuring out what's actually happening with club stuff vs. people's own plans."
claim_review_spans.R8: This does three things: it's warm without being a request, it asks a real informational question (which is easy to answer), and it clears up the ambiguity that confused you at the gathering. If they reply with something, you have a conversation. If they don't, you've lost almost nothing.
claim_review_spans.R9: **On the group chat:** you don't have to leave messages unread as a strategy. You can just... participate normally when something interests you, and not monitor whether people respond. The "waiting to be noticed" feeling is real, but it's a reason to lower the stakes of each message, not to opt out of the chat entirely.
claim_review_spans.R10: **On whether to go back to the club:** I wouldn't decide that while you're feeling raw. One more visit, with a different plan — arrive with one small goal, like asking one person a question about something concrete (what they're studying, how they found the club) rather than hoping to be invited into a group — is a much better test than one ten-minute sit.
claim_review_spans.R11: Two things would help me give you better advice: **what kind of club is it** (a hobby club, a cultural group, a department society?), and **how are you spending most of your non-class time right now**? Those two answers tell me where your realistic openings are.
